home.title: The women of the Fort de Romainville
home.lead: Resisters, hostages, deportees: many women passed through this fort in Les Lilas. This memorial gathers their traces, always showing where each piece of information comes from and what remains unknown.
home.slogan: Dusting off the history of these places
home.treeHelp: The trunk is time: from the opening of the camp in 1940, at the bottom, to the Liberation in 1944, at the top. Each branch is a year of arrival at the fort, each apple a woman.
home.treeHint: Hover or select an apple to discover a woman.
home.heroCredit: Entrance of the fort and watchtower, photograph taken at the Liberation – collection shared by the National memorial to women in the Resistance and Deportation
home.exploreTitle: Several paths into the memory of the fort

method.title: What we know, and what we don't
method.p1: The fort's archives are incomplete. One date may come from a German register, another from a memory told within a family. We don't treat them the same way: next to each piece of information, we show where it comes from and whether it could be checked.
method.p2: When a family does not want a person to be exposed, we keep only her name. In the tree, her apple stays empty.
method.sample: Example: how to read a record
method.missing: The casemate where she was held, and what became of her after the war.

story.title: Four years at the fort
story.lead: Scroll down to travel through the history of the camp, from its opening to the Liberation.
story.credit: Photographs: collection shared by the National memorial to women in the Resistance and Deportation
story.sources: Where does this information come from?

1.title: A fort becomes a camp
1.text: After the defeat of June 1940, the German army moved into the fort. From 1 November 1940, the first detainees were registered. Watchtowers went up and barbed wire ran along the rampart walk: it was the first German camp set up in occupied France.
1.alt: Barbed wire in front of a row of the fort's casemates

2.title: The hostage camp
2.text: From summer 1942, the fort held the hostages of the Paris region. On 21 September 1942, 46 hostages taken from the fort were shot at Mont-Valérien. In all, 209 detainees who passed through the fort were shot during the Occupation.

3.title: The “31000” convoy
3.text: 230 women, most of them in the Resistance, were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Among them were Charlotte Delbo, Danielle Casanova, Marie-Claude Vaillant-Couturier and Maï Politzer. Only 49 came back.
3.alt: Memorial plaques at the entrance of the fort, including the one for the convoy of 24 January 1943

4.title: The women's camp
4.text: The fort became the camp for women to be deported. More than 3,800 women were held there during the war; over 90% were then deported, mainly to Ravensbrück.
4.alt: Dormitory set up in a casemate

5.title: A tragic liberation
5.text: On 15 August, the last convoy left from Pantin station. On 20 August, as it fled, the garrison shot eleven resistance fighters and civilians. The next day, residents found their bodies behind the central building.
5.alt: Entrance of the fort and its watchtower, photographed at the Liberation
